That's how it should work. Someone (anyone) releases code and the community adopts/rejects it based on experience with the team, the case made for/against the update, etc.

If we wrote a client that forked to give us billions of Doge, you'd tell us to get knotted, right? So it wouldn't ever get through.

If we add in sidechain functionality for Doge/Eth tokens, you'll probably accept it.

However, we have to negotiate with EVERYONE for this.

The whole thing where the exchange tries to sue the developers for not hard forking is insane.

You want a hard fork, you write the code and release it. That's it. We're not the gatekeepers, the community is.

This is important because single points of failure are what cryptocurrency is meant to defend against. If @dogecoin was ever hacked, heaven forbid, I'd want to know you guys would realise it was talking nonsense and make good decisions.
The Doge/Eth bridge work is being done by an entirely independent team, who are even funded via Eth rather than Doge. We have status meetings from time to time, but neither of us leads the other.

@Bitcoin Dogecoin for example has multiple different teams doing different things. Max, Patrick & myself working Dogecoin Core. The reddit mods are an independent team we get along well with, but we have to negotiate changes with them.

Key point is, you should expect (and demand) this level of transparency from all cryptocurrency projects.

So any time someone says we're doing something with funds, look at that pot. If it hasn't moved, ask where the money is coming from.

Generally we announce expenditure on /r/dogecoin on reddit too.

Now, that pot in theory will at some point pay the devs back for a bunch of infrastructure we're running, but for the most part it doesn't move between releases because it pays out on releases. That's a standard we hold ourselves to, and you can hold us to it as well.
